uni-mtech-core-a.title: M.Tech Core I · Advanced Algorithms, VLSI & Power Systems
uni-mtech-core-a.description: M.Tech/ME core at graduate depth: advanced algorithms (DP, flows, randomised analysis, graph algorithms), VLSI design (CMOS power, Elmore delay, timing, ASIC flow) and power systems (per-unit, power flow, faults, protection), with code and numerical labs.

courses.title: Advanced Algorithms (M.Tech)
courses.summary: Dynamic programming, network flows, randomised analysis and shortest paths, each with a coding or numerical lab.
outcomes: Learners can design DP recurrences and implement them
Learners can compute max flow and min cut
Learners can analyse expected running time of randomised quicksort
Learners can implement Dijkstra with a heap

scenes.text: A bioinformatics team compares two reads to find their longest common subsequence.
The same DP powers git diff.

steps.title: Recurrence
steps.body: L[i][j] = L[i−1][j−1]+1 if xᵢ = yⱼ, else max(L[i−1][j], L[i][j−1]); L[0][*]=L[*][0]=0. Time and space O(mn); space reducible to O(min(m,n)) for the length.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: X = AGGTAB, Y = GXTXAYB → LCS = GTAB, length **4**.

steps.title: DP design checklist
steps.body:
- Define the subproblem precisely
- Write the recurrence and base cases
- Choose evaluation order
- Reconstruct the solution by backtracking

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing subsequence (gaps allowed) with substring.
- Off-by-one in table indices.

activity.prompt: Read two strings (one per line) and print the length of their longest common subsequence.
activity.starter:
a = input().strip()
b = input().strip()
# build DP table
activity.solution:
a = input().strip()
b = input().strip()
L = [[0]*(len(b)+1) for _ in range(len(a)+1)]
for i in range(1, len(a)+1):
    for j in range(1, len(b)+1):
        L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1]+1 if a[i-1]==b[j-1] else max(L[i-1][j], L[i][j-1])
print(L[len(a)][len(b)])

scenes.text: A city water board asks how much water can move from reservoir s to tank t.
The answer equals the capacity of the smallest cut.

steps.title: Ford–Fulkerson
steps.body: Repeatedly find an augmenting path in the residual graph and push the bottleneck. Edmonds–Karp (BFS paths) runs in O(VE²). **Max-flow = min-cut** (capacity of the cheapest s–t cut).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Edges: s→a 10, s→b 5, a→b 15, a→t 5, b→t 10.
Paths: s-a-t (5), s-a-b-t (5), s-b-t (5) → **15**. Cut {s}|rest = 10+5 = 15 confirms optimality.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting reverse residual edges (flow cancellation).
- Counting edges from T back to S in a cut capacity.

activity.prompt: Network: s→a 10, s→b 5, a→b 15, a→t 5, b→t 10. What is the maximum flow from s to t?

story.title: Why the library uses random pivots

scenes.text: An adversary feeds sorted data to a first-element-pivot quicksort: O(n²).
Random pivots make the expected cost ≈ 1.39 n log₂ n on any input.

steps.title: Indicator-variable proof
steps.body:
Elements of rank i<j are compared iff the first pivot from {i..j} is i or j: probability 2/(j−i+1). Summing:

**E[C] = 2(n+1)Hₙ − 4n ≈ 2n ln n**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying randomised quicksort is O(n log n) worst case — it is expected.
- Summing probabilities over all pairs without the 2/(j−i+1) factor.

activity.prompt: Using E[C] = 2(n+1)Hₙ − 4n with H₁₀₀₀ = 7.48547, compute the expected comparisons of randomised quicksort for n = 1000.

scenes.text: An emergency dispatch system needs shortest travel times from the hospital to every junction.
Dijkstra with a binary heap answers in O((V+E) log V).

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Set dist[s]=0; repeatedly extract the vertex with smallest tentative distance and relax its edges. Correct for **non-negative** weights; with negative edges use Bellman–Ford (O(VE)).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Edges (undirected): 0-1 4, 0-2 1, 2-1 2, 1-3 1, 2-3 5. Distances from 0: [0, 3, 1, 4].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Dijkstra with negative edges.
- Not skipping stale heap entries.

activity.prompt: Implement Dijkstra from vertex 0 on the undirected graph with edges 0-1:4, 0-2:1, 2-1:2, 1-3:1, 2-3:5. Print distances to vertices 0..3 separated by spaces.
activity.starter:
import heapq
edges = [(0,1,4),(0,2,1),(2,1,2),(1,3,1),(2,3,5)]
n = 4
# build adjacency and run Dijkstra
activity.solution:
import heapq
edges = [(0,1,4),(0,2,1),(2,1,2),(1,3,1),(2,3,5)]
n = 4
adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for u,v,w in edges:
    adj[u].append((v,w)); adj[v].append((u,w))
d = [float('inf')]*n; d[0] = 0
pq = [(0,0)]
while pq:
    du,u = heapq.heappop(pq)
    if du > d[u]: continue
    for v,w in adj[u]:
        if du+w < d[v]:
            d[v] = du+w; heapq.heappush(pq,(d[v],v))
print(' '.join(map(str,d)))
activity.hint: Skip entries whose popped distance exceeds d[u].

courses.title: VLSI Design (M.Tech)
courses.summary: CMOS power, interconnect delay, static timing analysis and the ASIC flow from RTL to GDSII, with numerical labs.
outcomes: Learners can compute dynamic CMOS power
Learners can compute Elmore delay of RC networks
Learners can compute max clock frequency from timing parameters
Learners can order the ASIC physical design flow

scenes.text: A mobile SoC team must cut 20% power without losing performance.
Because P ∝ V², a small voltage drop is the biggest lever.

steps.title: Power components
steps.body:
- **Dynamic:** P = α C V² f (α = activity factor)
- **Short-circuit:** both networks conduct briefly during transitions
- **Leakage:** subthreshold, gate and junction leakage, rising sharply at small nodes and high temperature

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
α=0.1, C=1 nF switched capacitance, V=1.0 V, f=2 GHz: P = 0.1×10⁻⁹×1×2×10⁹ = **0.2 W**.
DVFS to 0.8 V and 1.6 GHz: 0.1×10⁻⁹×0.64×1.6×10⁹ = 0.102 W (≈49% saving).

steps.title: Low-power techniques
steps.body: Clock gating (reduces α), power gating (cuts leakage), multi-Vt cells, DVFS.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating power as linear in V.
- Forgetting α (not every node toggles every cycle).

activity.prompt: Compute dynamic power for α = 0.1, C = 1 nF, V = 1.0 V, f = 2 GHz, in watts.

quiz.q: Halving V (same f) changes dynamic power by

scenes.text: A signal crossing the die arrives late; the wire is now slower than the gates.
Elmore delay gives a quick, pessimistic-but-useful estimate.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: For an RC tree, delay to node i: **τᵢ = Σₖ C_k · R_shared(i,k)**, where R_shared is resistance common to the paths from source to i and to k. For a ladder: τ_N = Σ_k R_k (Σ_{j≥k} C_j).

steps.title: Solved example · 2-segment ladder
steps.body: R₁=R₂=1 kΩ, C₁=C₂=10 fF: τ₂ = R₁(C₁+C₂) + R₂C₂ = 20 ps + 10 ps = **30 ps**.

steps.title: Distributed wire
steps.body: Uniform wire with total R, C: τ ≈ RC/2 — quadratic in length. Repeaters make delay linear in length.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying total R by total C (overestimates by 2× for distributed lines).
- Ignoring driver resistance and load capacitance.

scenes.text: An STA report shows a worst path of 400 ps combinational logic.
Add clock-to-Q and setup — does it meet timing?

steps.title: Setup and hold
steps.body:
Setup: T_clk ≥ t_clk-q + t_comb,max + t_setup − t_skew (skew positive when capture clock arrives later).
Hold: t_clk-q + t_comb,min ≥ t_hold + t_skew. Hold violations are frequency-independent — fix with delay buffers.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: t_clk-q = 50 ps, t_comb = 400 ps, t_setup = 30 ps, skew 0: T_min = 480 ps → f_max = **2.08 GHz**. At 2 GHz (500 ps) slack = +20 ps.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trying to fix hold violations by slowing the clock.
- Ignoring OCV/derates in sign-off corners.

activity.prompt: t_clk-q = 50 ps, worst combinational delay = 400 ps, setup = 30 ps, zero skew. What is f_max in GHz (2 decimals)?

courses.title: Power Systems (M.Tech)
courses.summary: Per-unit analysis, power transfer and load flow, symmetrical fault calculation and protection schemes with numerical labs.
outcomes: Learners can convert impedances to per-unit
Learners can compute real power transfer across a line
Learners can compute three-phase fault currents
Learners can match protection schemes to equipment

scenes.text: A state transmission utility studies a 132 kV line with 50 Ω series reactance.
Per-unit values make transformers disappear from the arithmetic.

steps.title: Bases
steps.body: Choose S_base (3-phase MVA) and V_base (line kV). Then **Z_base = kV²/MVA**, I_base = S_base/(√3 V_base). Z_pu = Z/Z_base. Change of base: Z_new = Z_old (S_new/S_old)(V_old/V_new)².

steps.title: Change of base
steps.body: Transformer 0.08 pu on 50 MVA → on 100 MVA: 0.08×100/50 = 0.16 pu.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using phase voltage with 3-phase MVA.
- Forgetting to change base for equipment rated differently.

activity.prompt: On a 100 MVA, 132 kV base, convert a 50 Ω line reactance to per-unit (3 decimals).

quiz.q: Per-unit transformer impedance on its own base is
0.1 pu on 20 MVA to 100 MVA base

lessons.title: Lab: Power transfer and load flow

scenes.text: At 7 PM demand peaks; the grid operator watches the angle between two buses.
P = V₁V₂ sinδ/X tells how close the line is to its limit.

steps.title: Power angle equation
steps.body: For a lossless line: **P = (V₁V₂/X) sin δ**, Q₁₂ = (V₁² − V₁V₂ cos δ)/X. Max transfer at δ = 90° (steady-state limit). Real power follows angle; reactive power follows voltage magnitude.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: V₁ = V₂ = 1.0 pu, X = 0.5 pu, δ = 30°: P = 2 sin30° = 1.0 pu = **100 MW** on 100 MVA base. P_max = 200 MW.

steps.title: Load flow methods
steps.body: Bus types: slack, PV, PQ. Gauss–Seidel (simple, slow), Newton–Raphson (quadratic convergence, Jacobian), fast-decoupled (exploits P–δ / Q–V decoupling).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using degrees in a calculator set to radians.
- Treating Q as controlled by angle.

activity.prompt: V₁ = V₂ = 1.0 pu, X = 0.5 pu, δ = 30°, base 100 MVA. Real power transferred in MW?

scenes.text: A 3-phase fault at an 11 kV bus must be cleared by a breaker.
Its interrupting rating must exceed the fault current.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Prefault voltage 1.0 pu. I_f = 1/Z_th (pu) for a bolted 3-phase fault. Multiply by I_base. Fault MVA = S_base/Z_th.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Generator X'' = 0.2 pu, transformer 0.1 pu (100 MVA base), fault at 11 kV side through both: Z = 0.3 pu → I_f = 3.333 pu. I_base = 5249 A → **17.5 kA**. Fault level = 333 MVA.

steps.title: Unsymmetrical faults
steps.body: Use sequence networks: SLG fault I_f = 3/(Z₁+Z₂+Z₀); LL: √3/(Z₁+Z₂) magnitude. SLG can exceed 3-phase fault if Z₀ is small.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using steady-state X instead of subtransient X'' for breaker sizing.
- Forgetting the DC offset (asymmetry) multiplier.

activity.prompt: X'' = 0.2 pu plus transformer 0.1 pu (100 MVA base) in series to an 11 kV bus. Bolted 3-phase fault current in kA?

quiz.q: Fault MVA with Z_th = 0.25 pu, 100 MVA

scenes.text: A new 220/33 kV substation design comes for review.
You must assign the right protection to each piece of equipment.

steps.title: Schemes
steps.body:
- **Distance (impedance) relays:** transmission lines, zones 1–3
- **Differential:** transformers, generators, busbars (compare in vs out current)
- **Buchholz relay:** oil-filled transformers (gas from incipient faults)
- **Overcurrent (IDMT):** radial distribution feeders
- **Under-frequency load shedding:** system-wide frequency defence

steps.title: Zone settings
steps.body: Typical: zone 1 = 80% of line instantaneous, zone 2 ≈ 120% with ~0.3 s delay, zone 3 backup further with longer delay.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting zone 1 at 100% (overreach into next line due to CT/VT errors).
- Forgetting CT ratio mismatch and inrush in transformer differential.

activity.prompt: Assign each protection to the equipment or function it primarily protects.

courses.summary: Technical, scenario and HR interview rounds for M.Tech graduates (algorithms/software, VLSI, power), a capstone lab and a 20-question final.

scenes.text: A semiconductor firm and a product company interview M.Tech graduates the same day.
Both want structured thinking: define, compute, check.

steps.title: Answer pattern
steps.body: Clarify inputs → state approach and complexity → work an example → discuss edge cases.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: 'Max frequency with 50/400/30 ps?' → 480 ps → 2.08 GHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Coding before clarifying.
- Ignoring hold when asked about timing.

rounds.q: How would you find the shortest path in a road graph with non-negative weights, and what if some weights are negative?
rounds.model: Use Dijkstra with a binary heap, O((V+E) log V). With negative edges Dijkstra's finalisation is unsafe; use Bellman–Ford, O(VE), which also detects negative cycles.
followups: How do maps handle continent-scale graphs?

rounds.q: Explain setup and hold time and how you fix each violation.
rounds.model: Setup requires data to arrive before the capturing edge minus t_setup; fix by reducing logic depth, upsizing, retiming or lowering frequency. Hold requires data to stay stable after the edge; it is frequency-independent, fixed by inserting delay on short paths.

rounds.q: Your design misses its power budget by 25%. What do you try?
rounds.model: First profile where power goes (dynamic vs leakage, by block). Then apply clock gating to idle logic, DVFS for non-critical modes, high-Vt cells off critical paths and power gating for idle blocks, re-checking timing after each.
followups: What is the trade-off of high-Vt cells?

lessons.title: Lab: Scenario & HR interview · power utility

scenes.text: A transmission utility interviews for assistant engineers.
They ask about faults, safety and teamwork in control rooms.

steps.title: Safety first
steps.body: In every grid scenario mention isolation, earthing, permits to work and communication with the load despatch centre.

steps.title: What utilities value
steps.body: Calm procedure-following, clear logging, escalation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Proposing to re-energise before finding the cause.
- Ignoring safety procedures in answers.

rounds.q: A 220 kV line trips on distance zone 1 and auto-recloses successfully. What do you do?
rounds.model: Log the trip and reclose, read the relay's fault locator and disturbance record, inform the load despatch centre, and schedule a line patrol near the indicated distance since a successful reclose suggests a transient fault such as a bird or lightning flashover.
followups: What if it trips again on reclose?

rounds.q: Compute the fault current at an 11 kV bus with Z_th = 0.3 pu on 100 MVA.
rounds.model: I_f = 1/0.3 = 3.33 pu; I_base = 100 MVA/(√3 × 11 kV) ≈ 5249 A, so I_f ≈ 17.5 kA. The breaker's rating should exceed this with margin for DC offset.
followups: What changes for an SLG fault?

rounds.q: Tell us about your M.Tech thesis.
rounds.model: State the problem and why it matters, your method (simulation tool, data), the main quantified result, a limitation, and how it applies to the employer's work.

rounds.q: How do you handle a disagreement with a senior about a switching sequence?
rounds.model: Raise the concern immediately and specifically, refer to the approved switching procedure, pause if safety is at risk, and escalate respectfully to the shift in-charge; record it.
